name: Frauded vs unfrauded rating

lead: On looksmaxxing forums, a frauded photo is one taken with favourable angle, lighting, lens distance, expression or editing, while an unfrauded photo shows the face neutrally, the way others see it day to day. Rating threads often ask posters to supply unfrauded pictures so that feedback reflects their ordinary appearance.

The payoff is a clearer baseline. Members who post neutral photos typically receive comments on skin, hair, eye area or facial hair, and then use that to choose what to work on. Frauding itself is also discussed as a skill, since angle and lighting choices change how a face reads in photos.

paras: Posters upload front-facing and side photos in even light without squinting, tilting or filters, and sometimes put them beside their best photo to compare. Others reply with ratings and suggestions such as skincare, a different hairstyle or grooming changes. Some users also discuss deliberate frauding for dating-app or social photos.

Ratings come from anonymous forum members and vary widely, and some threads are blunt in tone. Users report that comparing frauded and unfrauded images can be discouraging, and posting face photos publicly carries ordinary privacy considerations.

angle.text: Unfrauded threads give members a baseline of how they look in ordinary conditions. Feedback then guides changes such as skincare or a new hairstyle. Frauding, in contrast, is used to present the best version of a face in photos.

lead: Frauded versus unfrauded rating is a convention in looksmaxxing forums such as looksmax.org. A frauded photo is one in which angle, lighting, expression or editing make the face look better than it usually does; an unfrauded photo is a neutral, unflattering-conditions image meant to represent how the person looks in daily life.[1][2]

The practice helps people improve their looks by giving them a realistic baseline. Posters who request ratings on unfrauded pictures say they want feedback on how they look every day rather than at their best, and replies often point to specific things to change, such as skin, hairstyle, eye area or facial hair.[1][3] One user who posted neutral photos listed planned changes including clearer skin, a better-fitting hairstyle and an improved eye area.[3]

The same vocabulary appears in other contexts: threads on how celebrities look in unedited video, on height frauding, and on users who describe a frauded photo as their public face.[2] No published studies use these terms, although research on photographs and attractiveness ratings exists more broadly.
infobox: Front and side photos, ratings, advice

paras: In rating threads, members post photographs and ask others to score them. A frauded picture uses flattering conditions; an unfrauded one is presented as an honest representation. One thread opens with the poster saying it is fair to show what they realistically look like daily and be rated against the flattering version.[1]

Other threads apply the idea to specific features, such as unfrauded side profiles, or to the unedited appearance of famous people. In one thread on actors and models filmed in harsh light at a film festival, the poster argued that skin looked much poorer than in edited images and said this motivated their own skincare work with tretinoin; another user replied that celebrities are mostly above average rather than exceptional.[2]

Requests for unfrauded pictures function as a norm for getting useful feedback. Posters sometimes add disclaimers about their photos, for example clarifying that a visible asymmetry is only the moment of the photo rather than a condition.[1] Replies range from short rating labels to suggestions on grooming, hair and skin.[3]

Frauding is also discussed as a deliberate practice, including angle choice, lighting and, in height contexts, footwear and posture. Forum users debate whether being found out is socially costly, with some arguing it matters only if the unfrauded appearance falls short.

lore.intro: Members use the terms to separate flattering photos from everyday appearance and often ask for brutal honesty in ratings.[1][3]
